---
title: "Negative-binomial regression"
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---

The negative-binomial distribution relaxes the Poisson mean–variance equality while retaining nonnegative integer support. We continue with Storme's French liaison counts and use the paper-aligned liaison-by-final-consonant interaction.

```{r}
#| label: load-storme-nb
#| echo: true
path <- "data/storme-liaison/storme-liaison-counts.csv"
if (file.exists(path)) {
  storme <- read.csv(path)
} else {
  url <- paste0("https://zenodo.org/api/records/12733801/files/",
                "study1-data.csv/content")
  source_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
  download.file(url, source_file, mode = "wb")
  stopifnot(unname(tools::md5sum(source_file)) ==
              "8a7788489b6820822cda3f338881f77e")
  raw <- read.csv(source_file, check.names = FALSE)
  storme <- aggregate(freqfilms2 ~ final_morph + FinalConsonant + Liaison,
                      raw, sum)
  storme$reconstructed_count <- as.integer(storme$freqfilms2 * 100)
  names(storme)[1:4] <- c("final_morpheme", "final_consonant", "liaison",
                          "frequency_per_million_sum")
}
storme$liaison <- factor(storme$liaison, levels = c("no", "yes"))
storme$final_consonant <- factor(storme$final_consonant)
additive <- MASS::glm.nb(reconstructed_count ~ liaison + final_consonant,
                         storme, control = glm.control(maxit = 100L))
interaction <- MASS::glm.nb(reconstructed_count ~ liaison * final_consonant,
                            storme, control = glm.control(maxit = 100L))
```

With mean $\mu_i$ and size $\theta$,

$$
\mathbb{E}[Y_i]=\mu_i,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[Y_i]=\mu_i+\frac{\mu_i^2}{\theta}.
$$

The log link keeps $\mu_i$ positive. The additive model's liaison coefficient is a common-ratio restriction:

```{r}
#| label: additive-nb-summary
#| echo: true
c(theta = additive$theta,
  additive_liaison_log_ratio = coef(additive)[["liaisonyes"]],
  additive_liaison_ratio = exp(coef(additive)[["liaisonyes"]]))
```

Storme's analysis includes the interaction, so a single common liaison ratio is not the paper-aligned result.

```{r}
#| label: interaction-nb-contrasts
#| echo: true
grid <- expand.grid(liaison = levels(storme$liaison),
                    final_consonant = levels(storme$final_consonant))
grid$fitted <- predict(interaction, newdata = grid, type = "response")
wide <- reshape(grid, idvar = "final_consonant", timevar = "liaison",
                direction = "wide")
wide$liaison_ratio <- wide$fitted.yes / wide$fitted.no
wide
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-nb-fit
#| echo: true
library(ggplot2)
sampled <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  split(storme, interaction(storme$liaison, storme$final_consonant)),
  function(x) if (nrow(x) <= 240L) x else x[seq(1L, nrow(x), length.out = 240L), ]
))
ggplot(sampled, aes(liaison, reconstructed_count)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = .12, height = 0),
             size = .35, color = "grey45") +
  geom_point(data = grid, aes(y = fitted), color = "#1F5A85", size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    transform = "log1p",
    breaks = c(0, 10, 1000, 100000, 1000000), # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
    labels = c("0", "10", "1k", "100k", "1m") # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ final_consonant) +
  labs(x = "Liaison status", y = "Reconstructed token count (log1p scale)") +
  theme_classic()
```

Liaison cells have higher fitted means for each represented consonant, but the ratios are strongly consonant-specific. The response is reconstructed from frequency values, and lexical rows may remain dependent. Thus this population fit illustrates the paper's formula without reproducing its Bayesian uncertainty or establishing an independent causal liaison effect.
